entry: Constituent country of the [[Kingdom of the Netherlands]] occupying the southern 44% of the island of [[Saint Martin (island)|Saint Martin]] in the [[Caribbean]] (pop., 2023: 58,477). Its capital is Philipsburg. Its name is Dutch for Saint Martin. Formerly one of the island territories of the Netherlands Antilles, it became a constituent country on October 10, 2010, and has the status of an EU overseas country, though it is not part of the European Union. Category 5 Hurricane Irma caused widespread and significant damage on September 6–7, 2017.

Most populous city in [[South Dakota]] and county seat of Minnehaha County (pop., 2020: 192,517). Chartered in 1856 on the banks of the Big Sioux River, the city sits at the junction of Interstates 29 and 90. The falls, created about 14,000 years ago during the last ice age, drew Indigenous peoples, including the [[Sioux]]. The town was evacuated in August 1862 after two local settlers were killed in the Dakota War of 1862. Its economy is driven by financial services, healthcare, distribution and logistics, and advanced [[Manufacturing|manufacturing]].

Groups of Native American tribes and First Nations people of the [[Great Plains]]. The Sioux call themselves the Očhéthi Šakówiŋ, or "Seven Council Fires." The name Sioux is an exonym from a French transcription of the [[Ojibwe]] term Nadowessi. Before the 17th century the Santee Dakota lived around [[Lake Superior]], and the Dakota–Ojibwe War pushed them west into southern [[Minnesota]]. After the Dakota War of 1862 they were exiled from Minnesota and placed on reservations in Nebraska, North Dakota and South Dakota. The Lakota, the westernmost Sioux, defeated the 7th Cavalry Regiment at the Battle of Little Big Horn in 1876. Armed conflict with the [[United States]] ended with the [[Wounded Knee Massacre]] in 1890. A 1980 Supreme Court ruling found that the government had illegally taken Sioux lands. The payment owed, more than $1 billion as of 2018, has been refused in favor of the return of the Black Hills.

British post-punk rock band formed in London in 1976 by vocalist Siouxsie Sioux and bassist Steven Severin. Their debut album, *The Scream* (1978), received widespread acclaim. They achieved success as an alternative pop group in the 1980s, with *Kaleidoscope* (1980) peaking at number 5 on the UK Albums Chart. The pop single "Kiss Them for Me" gave them a mainstream U.S. hit in 1991. They were cited as an influence by [[Joy Division]], [[The Cure|the Cure]], [[U2]] and [[Radiohead]]. The band disbanded in 1996.

Device, usually a tube bent into an inverted U shape, that lifts liquid above the surface of a [[Reservoir|reservoir]] and discharges it lower, powered by gravity with no pump. The traditional explanation holds that [[Atmospheric pressure|atmospheric pressure]] pushes the liquid up into the reduced pressure at the top, as in a [[Barometer|barometer]]. Gravity siphons also work in a [[Vacuum|vacuum]], so a cohesion tension theory has been advanced, and both explanations may hold under different pressures. Egyptian reliefs from 1500 BC depict siphons drawing liquid from storage jars, and [[Hero of Alexandria]] wrote about them in *Pneumatica*. In a Venturi siphon, a second fluid is drawn into a fast-moving stream, the principle behind the carburetor of a gasoline engine.

Humanlike female being in [[Greek mythology]] with an alluring voice. Sirens appear in [[Homer]]'s *Odyssey*, where [[Odysseus]] saves his crew from their song. By the 7th century BC they were regularly depicted as human-headed birds, and the male siren disappeared from art around the fifth century BC. Sirens were later often portrayed as [[Mermaid|mermaids]], a form that became iconic in the medieval period. In medieval Christian art they symbolized the dangerous temptation embodied by women. "Siren" is also slang for a woman considered both very attractive and dangerous.

Order of fully aquatic, herbivorous mammals, commonly called sea cows or sirenians. Sirenians belong to the clade Paenungulata with [[Elephant|elephants]] and hyraxes, and evolved in the [[Eocene]] about 50 million years ago. The two living families are Dugongidae, which contains the dugong and the extinct Steller's sea cow, and Trichechidae, which contains three [[Manatee|manatee]] species. Sirenians have heavy bones that act as ballast, and they use strong lips to pull up seagrasses. They grow to between 2.5 and 4 metres (8.2 and 13.1 feet) in length. Steller's sea cow, the largest known sirenian, reached 10 metres (33 feet) and was driven to extinction by overhunting in 1768. They are also called sirens, after the [[Siren (mythology)|sirens]] of Greek mythology.

Palestinian-Jordanian assassin of U.S. senator and presidential candidate [[Robert F. Kennedy]]. On June 5, 1968, Sirhan shot Kennedy at the Ambassador Hotel in [[Los Angeles]], moments after Kennedy's victory in the California Democratic primary. Convicted of first-degree murder in 1969, he was sentenced to death, but the sentence was commuted to life imprisonment in 1972. In 1989 Sirhan said his only connection to Kennedy was Kennedy's support of Israel. Critics have questioned whether he acted alone, citing ballistic analyses, though appellate courts have upheld his conviction. He has been repeatedly denied parole.

Brightest star in the night sky, in the southern constellation [[Canis Major]]. Its name derives from the Ancient Greek for "glowing" or "scorching." Sirius is a [[Binary star|binary]] system of Sirius A, a main-sequence star about twice the mass of the [[Sun]] and 25 times as luminous, and Sirius B, a faint [[White dwarf|white dwarf]] companion. The two orbit each other every 50 years, and the system lies 8.6 light-years from Earth. Sirius B was originally the more massive star; it became a red giant before collapsing into a white dwarf around 120 million years ago. The star's heliacal rising marked the flooding of the [[Nile]] for [[Ancient Egypt|Ancient Egyptians]] and the "dog days" of summer for the Greeks.

American actress and singer. Her breakthrough came as the telekinetic teenager in [[Brian De Palma]]'s horror film *Carrie* (1976), which earned her a first Academy Award nomination. She won an Academy Award and a Golden Globe for playing country singer Loretta Lynn in *Coal Miner's Daughter* (1980), singing the songs herself. Her other films include *Badlands* (1973) and *JFK* (1991). She received a star on the [[Hollywood Walk of Fame]] in 2012 and released the album *Hangin' Up My Heart* (1983).

American amusement park company headquartered in [[Charlotte, North Carolina]]. It was formed on July 1, 2024, through the merger of Cedar Fair and the former Six Flags company. It operates 34 properties in [[North America]], including 20 [[Amusement park|amusement parks]] and 14 water parks, and manages two parks in [[Saudi Arabia]]. It is the largest regional amusement park operator in North America and the fifth largest in the world by attendance, with 47.4 million guests in 2025. It holds exclusive theme park rights to Warner Bros. properties such as [[Looney Tunes]] and [[DC Comics]].

Period of Chinese history from AD 304 to 439 in which the [[Jin dynasty (266–420)|Jin dynasty]] fragmented into short-lived states in northern China. Most were founded by non-Han peoples, mainly the Five Barbarians (Xiongnu, Xianbei, Di, Jie and Qiang), and most claimed the [[Mandate of Heaven]]. Rebels toppled the Jin court at [[Luoyang]] in 311 and Chang'an (modern-day [[Xi'an]]) in 316. From 376 to 383 the Former Qin unified northern and northwest China and [[Sichuan]], but its attempt to conquer southern China was stopped by the Eastern Jin. As many as nine states coexisted in the north in 400. The period ended in 439, when the Xianbei Northern Wei unified the north.

Strait between Denmark, [[Norway]] and [[Sweden]], connecting the [[North Sea]] with the [[Kattegat]]. Its name likely derives from Skagen, a Danish town near the northern cape of Denmark. It is 240 km long and 80–140 km wide, deepening toward the Norwegian coast, where the Norwegian Trench reaches over 700 m. Until the Eider Canal was built in 1784, it was the only access to the [[Baltic Sea]]. One of the world's busiest straits, it carries heavy shipping and supports an intensive fishing industry. It is a habitat for approximately 2,000 marine species, including Atlantic cod. [[Oslo]] and [[Gothenburg]] are the only large cities in its region, and environmental institutions have expressed concern about pressure from human activity and [[Climate change|climate change]]. The strait held strategic importance for Germany during both World Wars.

Albanian nobleman and military leader, the national hero of [[Albania]]. Sent as a hostage to the [[Ottoman Empire]] court, he entered the service of Sultan Murad II (r. 1421–1451) for the next twenty years. In 1443, during the Battle of Nish, he deserted the Ottomans and became ruler of Krujë. In March 1444 he established the League of Lezhë, uniting the Albanian principalities. In 1451 he recognized the sovereignty of the [[Naples|Kingdom of Naples]] over Albania, while remaining a de facto independent ruler. He fought the Ottomans until his death and is ranked among the most persistent opponents of their expansion. He became a central figure of the Albanian National Awakening in the 19th century.

Cartilaginous fish of the family Rajidae, a group of rays with flat bodies and stiff snouts. More than 150 species have been described, in 17 genera. Skates belong to the [[Chondrichthyes|cartilaginous fishes]], and their flat bodies and pectoral fins let them swim and colonize the sea floor. Their mouths are on the underside, while dorsal spiracles let them breathe while partly buried in sediment. They produce their young in cases called mermaid's purses, which differ between species and help identify them. The skate body plan arose about 286–221 million years ago, when skates diverged from [[Shark|sharks]].

Action sport in which riders perform tricks on a skateboard, also practiced as recreation, art and transport. It originated in the United States, where [[Surfing|surfers]] in California began "sidewalk surfing" in the late 1940s or early 1950s, when the waves were flat. The first manufactured skateboards were ordered by a [[Los Angeles]] surf shop. The first skateboarding magazine, *The Quarterly Skateboarder*, appeared in 1964. [[Polyurethane]] wheels, introduced in the early 1970s, improved traction and enabled vertical ramp riding. A 2009 report estimated the market at $4.8 billion in annual revenue. Skateboarding made its Olympic debut at the 2020 Summer Olympics in [[Tokyo]] and was included in the 2024 games. Since the 1970s, skateparks have been built for the sport, which is controversial where it has damaged curbs, benches and plazas, although the activity is legal.

One of three types of [[Vertebrate|vertebrate]] muscle tissue, the others being cardiac and smooth muscle. Skeletal muscles are usually attached by [[Tendon|tendons]] to the bones of the [[Skeleton]] and appear striated because of their [[Sarcomere|sarcomeres]]. Each muscle fiber is a long, multinucleated cell formed by the fusion of myoblasts, and it contains many [[Mitochondria|mitochondria]] to meet its energy needs. Sarcomeres, the basic contractile units of the fiber, are composed of actin and myosin filaments. The human body has more than 600 skeletal muscles, which produce movement, maintain posture, control body temperature and stabilize joints. Muscles are powered mainly by the oxidation of fats and carbohydrates, which produces [[Adenosine triphosphate|ATP]]. Skeletal muscle is also an endocrine organ.

[[Woman]] or girl who shares a parent or parents with another individual; a female [[Sibling|sibling]]. The male counterpart is a [[Brother]]. A full sister is a first-degree relative. The English word derives from Old Norse *systir*. Some publishers prefer "female sibling" to avoid equivocation, as the term has broadened colloquially to include non-relatives. Studies have found that older sisters tend to form close bonds with younger siblings, and that boys with older sisters were less likely to be delinquent. In a study in Perth, Australia, girls with only younger brothers lost their virginity on average more than a year later than average.

Chapel in the Apostolic Palace, the [[Pope|pope]]'s official residence in [[Vatican City]]. It takes its name from Pope Sixtus IV, who had it built between 1473 and 1481, and it is the site of papal conclaves that elect new popes. Renaissance painters including [[Sandro Botticelli]] decorated its walls with frescoes of the Life of [[Moses]] and the Life of Christ, completed in 1482. Between 1508 and 1512, under [[Pope Julius II]], [[Michelangelo]] painted the ceiling, a project that changed the course of Western art. He later painted *The Last Judgment* (1535–1541) on the altar wall. The chapel was consecrated on August 15, 1483, when it was dedicated to the Virgin Mary.

King of Ephyra (now Corinth) in [[Greek mythology]], condemned to push a boulder up a hill forever. He revealed Zeus's abduction of Aegina to her father, the river god Asopus, and cheated death twice. The gods condemned him to roll the boulder up the hill, only for it to roll back down each time it neared the top. Tasks that are laborious and never-ending are therefore called Sisyphean. [[Homer]]'s *Odyssey* describes Odysseus witnessing the punishment, and [[Albert Camus]] used the myth in his essay *The Myth of Sisyphus*.

Hindu goddess and female protagonist of the [[Ramayana]], consort of [[Rama]] and regarded as an avatar of [[Lakshmi]]. Adopted daughter of King Janaka of Videha, she is abducted in exile by the Rakshasa king [[Ravana]] and held in Lanka until Rama rescues her. In some versions she undergoes an *agni pariksha*, an ordeal of fire, to prove her chastity. Later, after a doubt about her fidelity, Rama sends her away while she is pregnant, and she gives birth to twins Kusha and Lava at the ashram of [[Valmiki]]. In the epic's conclusion she returns to the earth, her mother.

Indian plucked stringed instrument used in [[Hindustani classical music]]. Its name derives from the Persian *sehtar*, meaning three-stringed, and it developed in the [[Mughal Empire]] from the Persian *setar*. The earliest mention is in *Muraqqa-i-Dehli*, written in 1739. Most historians credit the 18th-century court figure Khusrau Khan with its invention; the older attribution to the poet [[Amir Khusrau]] is considered discredited. The instrument took its modern form in the late Mughal period, with a wider neck, a gourd body and metal frets. [[Ravi Shankar]] made the sitar known worldwide from the late 1950s, and the psychedelic culture of the 1960s brought it into Western pop through [[The Beatles]] and [[The Rolling Stones]].

[[Comedy]] genre for [[Radio|radio]] and [[Television|television]] centered on a recurring cast of characters in a consistent setting, such as a home or workplace. Unlike sketch comedy, which changes characters and settings in each skit, sitcoms maintain plot continuity across episodes. The term was not commonly used until the 1950s, when early programs were often filmed before a live studio audience, a format still used by [[The Big Bang Theory]]. Since the 1990s, animated sitcoms such as *The Simpsons* and *Family Guy* have expanded the genre. Many contemporary American sitcoms use a single-camera setup and no laugh track.

Hunkpapa Lakota leader who resisted United States government policies. Before the [[Battle of the Little Bighorn]], he had a vision of soldiers falling upside down into the Lakota camp, which his people took as a sign of victory. In June 1876 the Lakota and Northern Cheyenne defeated the 7th Cavalry under [[George Armstrong Custer]]. Sitting Bull led his band north into [[Saskatchewan]] in 1877 and surrendered in 1881, then performed with Buffalo Bill's Wild West show. In 1890 Indian agency police, supported by U.S. troops, shot him during an attempt to arrest him on the Standing Rock Indian Reservation in [[South Dakota]], amid fears that he would support the Ghost Dance movement.

War of June 5–10, 1967, fought between [[Israel]] and a coalition of Arab states, primarily Egypt, Syria and [[Jordan]]. After Egypt, under [[Gamal Abdel Nasser]], announced the closure of the Straits of Tiran to Israeli shipping, Israel launched air strikes that destroyed nearly all of Egypt's air force. It then occupied the [[Sinai Peninsula]] and [[Gaza Strip]], the [[West Bank]] including East Jerusalem, and the [[Golan Heights]]. The war caused more than 15,000 Arab fatalities and fewer than 1,000 Israeli. Its territorial changes shaped the [[Middle East]] into the 21st century, and many of its consequences remain unresolved.
